issues.legal_issue: Permission for a transfer during consolidation must be granted unless the transfer conflicts with a concrete principle or proposal forming part of the consolidation scheme.
material_facts: The applicants sought permission to exchange plots in villages where consolidation proceedings were in progress.
The Settlement Officer refused permission, relying in part on the stage and workload of consolidation and on the applicants becoming larger landholders.
The record indicated that plots in some villages were in adjacent chaks, although the actual location of the plots remained for the Settlement Officer to examine.
issues.conclusion: A qualifying application must be allowed unless the proposed transfer is likely to defeat the consolidation scheme; that requires a conflict with a principle that has become final or a concrete proposal that has been confirmed. The applications were remitted for a decision under that standard.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 16-A(1) and (2) of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, the Settlement Officer must grant permission for a qualifying transfer unless satisfied, for recorded reasons, that it is likely to defeat the scheme. Sections 13, 14, 18, 19 and 23 identify the scheme’s principles and proposals and the stages at which they become final or confirmed. Section 15 sets out relevant principles for framing the scheme. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.transfer_permission_application_during_c: A tenure-holder applies for permission to transfer a plot or share while consolidation proceedings are underway.
predicates.concrete_conflict_with_final_scheme: The proposed transfer conflicts in a substantial and concrete manner with a principle that has become final or a proposal that has been confirmed.

issues.definition: When a tenure-holder seeks permission to transfer property during consolidation and the transfer does not concretely conflict with the final scheme, permission is granted.

issues.legal_issue: Administrative workload, the applicants’ size as landholders, and a general preference for larger chaks do not replace the required inquiry into conflict with the consolidation scheme.
material_facts: The Settlement Officer referred to the disruption and additional work that exchanges might cause in forming or adjusting chaks.
The Settlement Officer also reasoned that the applicants were already large landholders and would become larger, potentially affecting smaller landholders.
The High Court set aside the refusal, but directed reconsideration on the basis that the exchange would further the scheme by creating larger chaks.
issues.conclusion: The stated workload and landholding-size considerations were not germane grounds for refusing permission. The High Court was also wrong to direct reconsideration on the general assumption that larger chaks would further the scheme; the Settlement Officer had to determine whether a concrete conflict existed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16-A(2) permits refusal only where the proposed transfer is likely to defeat the scheme, understood by reference to the principles and proposals described in sections 13, 14 and 19 and made final or confirmed under sections 18 and 23. Section 15’s principles do not establish a categorical rule that larger chaks must be created. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.transfer_permission_application_during_c: A tenure-holder applies for permission to transfer a plot or share while consolidation proceedings are underway.
predicates.refusal_based_only_on_administrative_bur: The Settlement Officer refuses permission because of anticipated administrative work or the applicants’ existing or resulting size as landholders, rather than a concrete conflict with the scheme.
predicates.refusal_on_those_grounds_is_invalid: The refusal cannot stand on those grounds alone.

issues.definition: A refusal based only on anticipated administrative burden or the applicants’ landholding size is invalid when permission is sought during consolidation.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court cannot direct permission or constrain reconsideration by assuming that a proposed transfer will further consolidation without the required assessment of concrete conflict.
material_facts: The High Court set aside the Settlement Officer’s refusal and directed fresh consideration while stating that larger chaks would further the scheme.
The Supreme Court held that the Settlement Officer had to decide whether the transfer conflicted with a final principle or confirmed proposal and issue a reasoned decision.
The case reached the Supreme Court by appeal from the High Court’s judgment in the transfer-permission proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s direction was set aside, and the applications were remitted to the Settlement Officer to be decided according to the statutory standard.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 16-A(2), 13, 14, 18, 19 and 23 require the Settlement Officer to determine whether the transfer conflicts with a final principle or confirmed proposal, and to record the grounds for that determination. The Court stated that judicial intervention is attracted where there is an error apparent on the face of the record or similar infirmity. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.appeal_from_transfer_permission_directio: An appeal is brought from a reviewing court’s direction concerning an application for permission to transfer property during consolidation.
predicates.high_court_assumed_transfer_would_furthe: The reviewing court directs reconsideration on a general assumption about the transfer’s effect without leaving the responsible officer to assess concrete conflict with the scheme.
predicates.direction_set_aside_and_application_remi: The direction is set aside and the application is returned for determination under the governing standard.

issues.definition: On an appeal from a transfer-permission direction, a direction based on a general assumption rather than a concrete conflict assessment is set aside and the application is remitted.

issues.legal_issue: A later administrative order made mechanically to comply with a reviewing court’s direction does not bar an appeal challenging that direction and falls when the direction is set aside.
material_facts: After the High Court’s direction, the Settlement Officer granted permission without independently examining the application against the relevant principles and proposals.
The applicants argued that this later order had become final and prevented the appeal from providing relief.
The later order depended on and mechanically complied with the High Court’s direction.
issues.conclusion: The later order did not bar the appeal and was set aside along with the High Court’s direction.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the later order as wholly dependent on the direction under appeal; once that direction was set aside, the dependent order could not stand. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this procedural conclusion.

predicates.appeal_challenges_underlying_court_direc: An appeal challenges a court direction that formed the basis for a later administrative order.
predicates.later_administrative_order_depends_only_: The administrative officer issued the later order mechanically to comply with the court direction, without an independent examination.
predicates.later_order_does_not_bar_appeal_and_is_s: The later order does not prevent appellate relief and is set aside with the underlying direction.

issues.definition: When a later administrative order depends only on the direction under appeal, it does not bar the appeal and is set aside with that direction.
